regimens.indication: Treatment of Generalized and Partial Seizures (Maintenance Therapy)

refs.quote: INDICATIONS AND USAGE A. Sedative B. Anticonvulsant–For the treatment of generalized and partial seizures.

Adults: 60 to 200 mg/day. Pediatric Patients: 3 to 6 mg/kg/day. Special Patient Population –Dosage should be reduced in the elderly or debilitated because these patients may be more sensitive to barbiturates. Dosage should be reduced for patients with impaired renal function or hepatic disease.

regimens.dose_text: Adults: 60 to 200 mg/day (administered once daily at bedtime or in 2 to 3 divided doses). Dosage should be reduced in elderly or debilitated patients and patients with impaired renal function or hepatic disease. Therapeutic target: 15 to 40 mcg/mL.

refs.quote: Dosage should be reduced for patients with impaired renal function or hepatic disease.

renal_basis.note: Reduce dosage in patients with impaired renal function

hepatic.value: Phenobarbital is contraindicated in patients with marked impairment of liver function. Dosage should be reduced for patients with hepatic disease.

refs.quote: CONTRAINDICATIONS Phenobarbital is contraindicated in patients who are hypersensitive to barbiturates, in patients with a history of manifest or latent porphyria, and in patients with marked impairment of liver function or respiratory disease in which dyspnea or obstruction is evident.
Barbiturates depress the sensory cortex, decrease motor activity, alter cerebellar function, and produce drowsiness, sedation, and hypnosis.

mg_safety.note: CNS depressant effects of barbiturates can exacerbate respiratory muscle fatigue in myasthenia gravis; use with caution

value.instructions: Phenobarbital immediate-release tablets may be crushed and mixed with water or feeding solution for enteral tube administration.

refs.quote: The barbiturates are nonselective central nervous system (CNS) depressants that are primarily used as sedative-hypnotics. In sub-hypnotic doses, they are also used as anticonvulsants.

mechanism_of_action.value: Barbiturates depress the sensory cortex, decrease motor activity, alter cerebellar function, and produce drowsiness, sedation, and hypnosis. In high enough therapeutic doses, barbiturates induce anesthesia.

value.toxic_threshold: > 40 mcg/mL (somnolence, nystagmus, ataxia), > 60-80 mcg/mL (coma, respiratory arrest)
value.sampling_timing: Trough serum level immediately prior to dose after reaching steady state (due to long half-life of 79-118 hours, steady state is reached after 2 to 3 weeks)
value.notes: Potent hepatic microsomal enzyme inducer; enhances clearance of co-administered medications.

refs.quote: Anticonvulsant Use –Clinical laboratory reference values should be used to determine the therapeutic anticonvulsant level of phenobarbital in the serum. To achieve the blood levels considered therapeutic in pediatric patients, higher per-kilogram dosages are generally necessary for phenobarbital and most other anticonvulsants.

value: Sedation, drowsiness, and morning hangover effect
Paradoxical excitation, hyperactivity, or irritability (pediatrics and elderly)

refs.quote: The following adverse reactions and their incidence were compiled from surveillance of thousands of hospitalized patients who received barbiturates.

value: Life-threatening respiratory depression and hypoventilation (especially with IV administration or concomitant sedatives)
Severe physical and psychological dependence with life-threatening withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens
Exfoliative dermatitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Hypotension and cardiovascular collapse with rapid IV administration

refs.quote: The manifestations of a long-acting barbiturate in overdose include nystagmus, ataxia, CNS depression, respiratory depression, hypothermia, and hypotension.
Reports of infants suffering from long-term barbiturate exposure in utero included the acute withdrawal syndrome of seizures and hyperirritability from birth to a delayed onset of up to 14 days

contraception.value: Phenobarbital induces hepatic enzymes metabolizing estrogen and progestin, reducing oral contraceptive efficacy; recommend barrier or non-hormonal contraception.

refs.quote: An alternate contraceptive method might be suggested to women taking phenobarbital.

lactation_summary.value: Small amounts of barbiturates are excreted in milk. Caution should be exercised and infant monitored for somnolence and weight gain.

refs.quote: Caution should be exercised when phenobarbital is administered to a nursing woman, because small amounts of barbiturates are excreted in the milk.

value.effect: Potent induction of hepatic microsomal enzymes increases metabolism of oral anticoagulants, substantially lowering anticoagulant activity and PT/INR.
value.management: Monitor PT/INR closely when initiating, adjusting, or stopping phenobarbital; warfarin dosage requirements typically increase substantially.

refs.quote: Phenobarbital lowers the plasma levels of dicumarol and causes a decrease in anticoagulant activity as measured by the prothrombin time.

value.effect: Enhances clearance of exogenous corticosteroids via hepatic microsomal induction, potentially leading to treatment failure in neuroimmunologic disorders.
value.management: Adjust corticosteroid dosage upward when coadministering with phenobarbital and monitor clinical immunosuppressive response.

refs.quote: Barbiturates appear to enhance the metabolism of exogenous corticosteroids, probably through the induction of hepatic microsomal enzymes.

value.effect: Induces metabolic clearance of estrogen and progestin components, causing failure of contraception and breakthrough bleeding.
value.management: Advise female patients of childbearing potential to use alternative or additional non-hormonal barrier contraceptive methods.
